pages.text:
A fusion reactor can't melt down: lose control and the plasma goes out. But it goes out hard.
# Disruptions
Crossing a limit dumps the plasma's energy into the wall in an instant: heavy wear on the First Wall and Divertor (more for a hotter, bigger plasma), possibly a few blocks melted out of the vessel, which then has to be rebuilt. A vertical disruption jerks the vessel and can open a vacuum leak. A tokamak carrying a big current can make runaway electrons that burn through the wall at the midplane, breaking the vacuum and letting the plasma's tritium out.

# Quench
Coils warming while energised (out of Liquid Helium) quench; see Superconducting Magnets.
# Coolant loss
Without Water or Lead-Lithium flowing, the First Wall passes 1,300°C or the blanket 900°C: they wear fast, and well past it the plasma collapses and tiles melt.
# Vacuum leaks
A leak lets air in: the plasma can't start, and air in a hot vessel wears the wall. Idle seals bed back in slowly; the Remote Handling Arm reseals one.
# Tritium releases
Vented exhaust and a burnt-through wall release tritium, contaminating the air and ground round the reactor like fallout. Inside a containment it stays inside.

# Alarms
The Plasma page lights alarms for density, beta, vertical position, the pulse's end, vacuum, coolant, magnets, wear, disruption, quench and tritium. The serious ones sound a klaxon until you silence them.
